parole.significato: Forms nouns (typically of Latin or Greek stems, often corresponding to adjectives ending in -isk)
parole.testo: From French -ique, from Latin -icus.

parole.significato: similar to -era; -ize (makes a verb from a noun or adjective)
parole.testo: Borrowed from or equivalent to French -iser, corresponding to Latin ‑issāre and Ancient Greek -ίζειν (-ízein). -isera thus contains -era, borrowed from French -er, from Latin -āre.
From French -ier, -ière, from Latin -ārius, -ārium, -āris. Doublet of -är.
From French -aire, from Latin -ārius, -ārium, -āris. Doublet of -iär, -jär.

parole.significato: -ous; making an adjective from a noun
parole.testo: From French -eux, -euse, from Latin -ōsus, -ōsa.
Borrowed from French ablatif (“the ablative case”), from Latin ablativus (“the ablative case”), from ablātus (“taken away”), from auferō (“to take away”).
From French académie, from Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía).
Borrowed from French alliance, from allier, from Latin alligāre. Cognate of German Allianz.
From French amiral, from Medieval Latin amiralis, from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander”) + -alis (“-al”).
From older French amunition, rebracketing of la munition as l'amunition, from Latin munitio.
Borrowed from French animosité, from Latin animositas.
Borrowed from French applaudir, from Latin applaudere, superficially equivalent to applåd + -era.
From French apporte, the second-person singular imperative of French apporter, itself from Latin apporto. Compare German Apport.
Borrowed from French artificiel, from Latin artificiālis.

parole.significato: a baluster (a short column used in a group to support a rail)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French balustre, from Latin balaustium, from Ancient Greek βαλαύστιον (balaústion).
From French barrière, from Old French barriere, from barre, from Vulgar Latin *barra, possibly from Frankish *bara, from Proto-Germanic *barō.
Borrowed from French béton (“concrete”), from Latin bitūmen (“asphalt”), from Gaulish [Term?].

Borrowed from French bibliothèque, from Latin bibliothēca (“library”), originally from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “book-room”), from βιβλίον (biblíon, “book”) + θήκη (thḗkē, “box, chest”).
Borrowed from French blâmer, from Late Latin blasphēmāre (“blaspheme”).
From French brutal from Medieval Latin brutalis, from brūtus.

parole.significato: a small shop, typically larger than a kiosk but smaller than an affär, but need not restrict itself to foodstuffs
parole.testo: From French boutique, from Latin apotheca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē).

parole.significato: a homosexual male; gay, fag, queer, poof
parole.testo: Uncertain: * One proposed source is månsing bög (“dupe”). * Another is French bougre (“scoundrel”), from Medieval Latin Bulgarus (“heretic”). * also compare dialectal böj (“leather bag”).
From French certificat, from Latin certificatum.
Unadapted borrowing from French croissant, present participle of verb croître (“to grow”).
From French décimer suffixed with -era, from Latin decimāre.

Borrowed from French déprimer, from Latin dēprimere.
Borrowed from French dignité, from Latin dignitās.
Borrowed from French diplôme, from Latin dīplōma, from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, “folded paper, license”).
From French distrait, the past participle of distraire, from Latin distrahere.
Borrowed from French duel, from Latin duellum, from duo (“two”).
Borrowed from French échelon, from échelle, from Latin scāla. Doublet of skala.
Borrowed from French égide, from Latin aegis, from Ancient Greek αἰγίς (aigís).
Borrowed from French équivoque, from Latin aequivocus.
From French élémentaire, from Latin elementāris.
Borrowed from French énergie.
From French énorme, from Latin ēnōrmis.
From French exalté, from Latin exaltāre
From French exercice, from Latin exercitium.
Borrowed from French expédier, from Latin expedīre.
Borrowed from French familier, from Latin familiaris, equivalent to familj + -jär. First attested in 1643.
Borrowed from French fasciner suffixed with -era, from Latin fascinare, from Latin fascinum (“charm, spell, witchcraft”).

Borrowed from French flacon (“bottle”), from Middle French flascon, from Late Latin flascō, from Frankish *flaskā (“bottle, flask”), from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ. Doublet of flaska. First attested in 1868.
From French fleuriste, from Latin floris (“genitive singular of flōs, flower”), + -ist.
From French farce, from Vulgar Latin farsa, from Latin farcire (“cram; stuff”). Cognate of Danish fars, German Farce. Doublet of fars.
From French généreux, from Middle French genereux, from Latin generōsus, from genus (“birth, origin”) + -ōsus.
From French génie, from Latin genius.
Borrowed from French grâce, from Latin gratia. Doublet of graciös and gratis.
Borrowed from French habile, from Latin habilis.
Borrowed from French hérédité, from Latin hērēditās.
Borrowed from French honnête, from Old French honeste, from Latin honestus.
Borrowed from French honneur, from Latin honor.
From French hôtel, from Middle French hostel, from Old French ostel; inherited from Latin hospitāle.

First used in Swedish in 1638, from French humeur, same as English humour, Latin humor (“fluid”), having bodily fluids in good balance. The funny-haha-humour meaning (Swedish humor) is more recent, originating in England in Shakespeare's time.
Borrowed from French hybride, from Latin hybrida, influenced by Ancient Greek ὕβρις (húbris).
From French idée, from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see”). Doublet of idol and idyll.
Borrowed from French illégal, from Medieval Latin illēgālis.
Borrowed from French instructeur, from Latin īnstrūctor.
Borrowed from French irrégulier, from Late Latin irregulāris.
Borrowed from French jour (“day”), ultimately derived from Late Latin diurnum (“day”). First attested in 1886.
Borrowed from French calcul, from Latin calculus.

From French chanterelle, from New Latin cantharellus, from Latin cantharus + -ellus, a diminutive suffix.
Borrowed from French capacité, from Latin capacitas. Doublet of kapabel.

Borrowed from French carré, from Latin quadratus. Cognate of Danish karré, German Karree. Doublet of kvadrat.
Borrowed from French casser, from Latin quassāre. Cognate of German kassieren, Danish kassere.
Borrowed from French communiqué, from communiquer, from Latin commūnicāre. Doublet of kommunicera.
From French compagnie, from Vulgar Latin *compania, from Late Latin compāniō, from com- + pānis (with + bread). Doublet of kompanjon and kumpan.

parole.significato: ability to run long distances or perform other cardio; endurance, aerobic fitness
parole.testo: From French condition, from Latin conditio
Borrowed from French conducteur, from Latin condūcō (“combine, drag together”). Doublet of kondottiär.
Borrowed from French concurrence, from Latin concurrens. Cognate of German Konkurrenz, English concurrence, concurrency.
From French conséquence, from Latin consequentia.

parole.significato: a copy, a reproduction, a duplicate
parole.testo: From French copie, from Latin copia.
From French copier, from Medieval Latin copiare, kopiera.
Borrowed from French copieux, from Medieval Latin cōpiōsus, from Latin cōpia. Doublet of kopia.

parole.significato: a chorister (singer in a choir, particularly in a church or an opera)
parole.testo: From French choriste, from Latin chorista, equivalent to kor + -ist.
Borrowed from French corvette. Further origin disputed. Possibly from Latin corbīta or Dutch korf.

parole.significato: coryphée (orchestra conductor in Ancient Greek drama)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coryphée, from Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos), from κορῠφή (korŭphḗ).
Borrowed from French créer, from Latin creāre. Cognate of German kreieren. First attested in 1619.
Borrowed from French crever, from Latin crepare. Doublet of krepera.

Borrowed from French croûton, from croûte, from Latin crusta.
Borrowed from French culte, from Latin cultus. Doublet of kultur.
From French cultiver (suffixed with -era), from Medieval Latin cultivare, from Latin cultus. Cognate of English cultivate and German kultivieren.
From French couleur, from Latin color (“colour”).

parole.significato: a cousin (the child of a person's aunt or uncle)
parole.testo: From French cousin, from Latin consobrinus. Caused a semantic shift in the words syssling and brylling, formally meaning ”cousin” (on mother’s and father’s side, respectively), to their modern meanings second cousin and third cousin.

parole.significato: a quarter (one of four equal parts)
parole.testo: From French quart, from Latin quartus, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeturtos ~ *kʷetwr̥tos.
From French chœur, from Latin chorus.

parole.significato: prone to strong, unpredictable changes in mood, especially to violent anger; unstable, volatile, unbalanced, labile, et…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French labile, from Latin lābilis (“slippery”). Doublet of lapsus and lavin.
Borrowed from French langouste, from Latin locusta.
Borrowed from French légionnaire, from Latin legiōnārius.
From French lecture, from Latin lēctūra.
Borrowed from French lier, from Latin ligāre. Doublet of allians, legera, lian, liga, liktor, and reliabel.

parole.significato: liqueur (sweet, often fruit-flavored liquor – not to be confused with liquor)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French liqueur, from Latin liquor.
Borrowed from French littérateur, from Latin litterator.
Borrowed from French lugubre, from Latin lugubris, from Latin lugeo (“mourn”).
Borrowed from French lucratif, from Latin lucrativus.
Borrowed from French luxe, from Latin luxus.
Borrowed from French magnifique, from Latin magnificus.

Borrowed from French manœuvre, from Old French maneuvre, from Latin manuopera, derived from manu (ablative of manus (“hand”) and opera (plural of opus (“work”)). Compare English manoeuvre, manual, operation and operate in English.
From French machine, from Latin machina, from Ancient Greek μαχανά (makhaná). Laundry sense: clipping of tvättmaskin (“washing machine”).
Borrowed from French matériel, from Late Latin māteriālis, from Latin māterĭa (“matter”), from mater, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr (“mother”).
Borrowed from French matrice, from Latin mātrīx.

parole.significato: a melody (sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase)
parole.testo: From French mélodie. Compare also German Melodie, from Latin melodia.
Borrowed from French milice, from Latin mīlitia, from mīles (“soldier”). Doublet of militär.

parole.significato: ministry, cabinet (the set of ministers in a government)
parole.testo: From French ministère, from Latin ministerium.
From French mobile, from Latin mōbilis.
From French moderne, from Late Latin modernus.
Borrowed from French monocle, from Latin monoculus.
Borrowed from French mouiller, from Latin mollīre.

parole.significato: a municipality, a small, incorporated town (in ancient Rome or in Sweden c. 1862-1971)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French municipe, based on Latin mūnicipium, used in Swedish since 1929.

parole.significato: A mushroom belonging to the genus Tricholoma.
parole.testo: From French mousseron, from Old French mousseron, from Vulgar Latin [Term?].
From French musc, from Latin mūscus.
From French mystique, from Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystical”). First attested in 1749.
Borrowed from French mystère, from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion). Doublet of mysterium.
From French meuble, from Latin mōbilis.
From French nerveux, from Middle French nerfveux, from Old French nerveus, borrowing from Latin nervōsus.
Borrowed from French neveu, ultimately from Latin nepōs (“grandchild, nibling”), whence also English nephew.
Borrowed from French nièce, ultimately from Late Latin neptia, from Latin neptis (“granddaughter”), whence also English niece.
Borrowed from French niche, from Latin nīdus (“nest”).
Borrowed from French notice, from Latin nōtitia, from nōtus.
Borrowed from French obscur, from Latin obscurus.
Borrowed from French offensive, offensif, from Latin offendēre.

parole.significato: banking permit (license to conduct banking business)
parole.testo: From French octroi, from French octroyer, from Late Latin auctorizare.
Borrowed from French oculaire, from Latin ocularis, from oculus. Doublet of okular.
Borrowed from French originel, from Late Latin originālis (“primitive, original”), from Latin origō (“beginning, source, origin”). Doublet of original.
Borrowed from French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis).
From French parole (“word”), from Latin parabola (“parable”). Attested since 1798.
From Old Swedish parti, from French partie, parti, the past participle of French partir (“to divide”), from Latin partīre (“to part”). Doublet of party.
From French passion, ultimately from Latin passio.

parole.significato: a patriarchy, a social system dominated by men
parole.testo: From French patriarcat, from Medieval Latin patriarchatus, used since 1610.

parole.significato: a play, a piece (to be performed at a theater)
parole.testo: From French pièce, from Late Latin pettia, from Gaulish *pettyā, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis.
Borrowed French plastique.
Borrowed from French plomb, from Middle French plom, from Old French plom, from Latin plumbum. Attested since 1829.
Borrowed from French plume, from Latin pluma (“feather”).

From French police, from Late Latin polītīa
Borrowed from French ponton, from Latin pōns (“bridge”).
From French populaire, from Latin populāris. Compare Norwegian and Danish populær, English popular.

From French présenter, from Latin praesentāre (“to show, to present”).
From French princesse, from Vulgar Latin principissa, from Latin prīnceps.

From French ravine, from Latin rapīna.
Borrowed from French réception, English reception, from Latin receptio.

From French représaille, from Medieval Latin reprensaliæ, from Latin reprēndēre, from earlier Latin reprehendere.
Borrowed from French reste, from Latin restāre (“remain”).

parole.significato: a restaurant (an eating establishment in which diners are served food at their tables)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French restaurant. First attested in 1865.
From French résultat, from Medieval Latin resultatum, from the past participle of Medieval Latin resultāre.

parole.significato: retreat (falling back, of a military unit or more generally, sometimes figuratively)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French retraite, from retraire, from Latin retrahere.
Borrowed from French rigoureux, from Latin rigorōsus, from rigor. Doublet of rigid.
From French rituel, from Latin ritualis. Cognate of Danish rituel, German rituell.
Borrowed from French sens, from Latin sēnsus, from sentīre.
Borrowed from French séculariser, from Latin saeculāris. By surface analysis, sekulär + -isera.

parole.significato: serious (meant or worthy of being taken seriously)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sérieux, from Late Latin sēriōsus.
From French servir, from Latin servīre derived from servus (slave, servant).
Borrowed from French séreux, from Latin serosus, from serum. Cognate of German serös.
From French scalaire, from Latin scalaris. Doublet of skala and eskalera.
From French scandale, from Old French scandale, from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum, from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon).
From French ésprit (compare English sprite), from Old French esprit, from Latin spiritus (“air, breath”).
Borrowed from French substantiel, from Latin substantiālis. Cognate of German substanziell.

From French sulfate, from New Latin sulphatum, taken from the expression acidum sulphatum (“salt”), from sulphatus, from Latin sulphur (“sulfur”). The term was first used in 1787 by the French chemist L. B. G. De Morveau.
From French souverain, from Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super (“above”). Cognate of English sovereign, Italian soprano.

parole.significato: synchronous, simultaneous, aligned in time (phase) and tempo (frequency)
parole.testo: From French synchrone, from Latin synchronus, from Ancient Greek σύγχρονος (súnkhronos).

parole.significato: A party were the guests have consumed all served food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French table rase, derived from Latin tabula rasa, with the spelling changed to suit the French-style pronunciation.

parole.significato: a middle-aged or older (and usually more distant) female relative, an aunt
parole.testo: From French tante, from Old French ante (nominative form), from Latin amita, diminutive of Proto-Indo-European *amma-, *ama- (“mother”), a lost baby-word of the papa-type.
Borrowed from French terrain, from Latin terrēnum, from terrēnus, from terra.

parole.significato: A tome, a volume (in a series of books), a (thick) book.
parole.testo: Used in Swedish since 1697. From French tome, Latin tomus (“section of larger work”), from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “section, roll of papyrus, volume”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, separate”). Cognate with English tome.
From French torture, from Latin torquere. Attested from 1604.

Borrowed from French unicité, from Latin unicitas.
Borrowed from French uniformité, from Latin uniformitas. By surface analysis, uniform + -itet.
From French unique, from Latin unicus.
From French vague, from Latin vagus (“unsteady, wandering”).

parole.significato: the claimed value printed upon something
parole.testo: Borrowed from French valeur, derived from Latin valor. First attested in 1632.
From French vélocipède, from Latin velox (“rapid, prompt”) and pes (“foot”).

parole.significato: a vitrine (glass-paneled cabinet), a display cabinet
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vitrine (“shop window, vitrine, display case”), ultimately based on Latin vitrum (“glass”).
Borrowed from French vivacité, from Latin vivacitas.
Borrowed from French volontaire, from Latin voluntārius.
Borrowed from French vomir, from Latin vomere.
From French vulgaire, from Latin vulgāris, from Latin vulgus. Attested since 1842. Cognate of German vulgär.
Borrowed from French à (“to; at”). First attested in 1644.
